idiom_name: hand-rolled role/permission tables behind one rbac_allow(subject, action, object) decision function; Open Policy Agent sidecar for policy-as-data
implementation_notes: C has no authorization framework, so both the decision data and the decision function are hand-written. Fittingly for the classic RBAC0 shape, roles are often a bitmask over a fixed role enum (the subject's roles are the OR of role bits, a permission is the mask a role must carry) or, past the word width, a table of (subject, role) and (role, permission) rows. Either way route every protected operation through one decision function wrapped in a single guard so no call site evaluates rules itself, take the subject's roles from server-side session state and never from a request field, and deny on an unknown role, a null table or a failed lookup. Where policy values churn faster than the binary, the idiomatic modern shape is an Open Policy Agent sidecar: the guard POSTs {roles, action, resource} and enforces OPA's allow/deny JSON, keeping the decision in Rego data while the mediation seam stays in C - at the cost of a network call per decision, so cache with a bounded TTL and fail closed on timeout. nginx's auth_request module is the server-side realization of the same 'centralize the decision, delegate the enforcement' split.
pitfalls: A bitmask silently caps the role vocabulary at the width of the integer type; past 32/64 roles switch to (subject, role) rows or an OPA decision service before a new role wraps or vanishes.
Mutable role state in a global or session struct shared across threads needs a lock; a read racing a grant/revoke write decides against a half-updated mask.
Resolving the subject from a header, cookie or query parameter the session never verified makes the decision forgeable; source roles from server-side session state only.
A NULL policy table, a failed row lookup or a failed OPA HTTP call must resolve to deny - fail-open error handling turns a missing rule into access.
String-comparing role names with strcmp in the hot path is both a timing signal and an allocation trap; intern or hash role names once at load time.
